opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. You know, I've spent most of my career working on the foundations of machine learning: graphical models, variational autoencoders, equivariant neural networks, and so on. At some point you start asking yourself, what is all of this actually for? Where can these tools make the biggest difference in the world?

For me, the answer increasingly became the physical sciences, and materials in particular. If you look at the big challenges we face, climate change above all, so many of the solutions come down to materials. Better batteries, more efficient catalysts, sorbents that can pull carbon dioxide out of the air, membranes for separating gases, materials for hydrogen storage. These are all materials problems. Historically, discovering a new material has been painfully slow: lots of trial and error in the lab, often a decade or more from idea to product.

What's changed is that we now have the tools to really accelerate that. You can combine physics-based simulation, like density functional theory and molecular dynamics, with deep learning models that respect the symmetries of the physical world. That's where a lot of my work on equivariance comes in. On top of that, generative models can propose candidate structures rather than just screening ones you already have. So you get this loop: generate, simulate, predict properties, then go to the lab and validate. That loop can be orders of magnitude faster than before.

There's also something very satisfying, intellectually, about working at the intersection of physics and machine learning. My background is actually in theoretical physics, so in a way it feels like coming home. Physics gives you strong inductive biases, and machine learning gives you the flexibility to learn from data. Putting them together is, I think, one of the most exciting frontiers in AI right now.

As for CuspAI specifically, I felt the time was right to do this in a startup rather than purely in academia or a big tech lab. To really have an impact, you need to close the loop with the real world: work with partners, actually make materials, and get them deployed. A focused company, with a great team and a clear mission around materials for climate and energy, is the best vehicle for that. Honestly, at this stage of my career I want to work on something where, if it succeeds, it genuinely matters for the planet. Materials discovery is that thing for me.

r001.rationale: The response cites climate change and materials as reasons to pursue solutions, but does not mention political difficulty in addressing climate change.

r002.rationale: It describes the intellectual satisfaction of combining physics and machine learning and the practical goal of developing materials that benefit the planet.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've spent most of my career working on the machinery of machine learning, variational inference, Bayesian methods, graph networks, equivariance, and at some point you ask yourself: what is all this machinery actually for? I've always been a physicist at heart. I did my PhD in theoretical physics, and I think of AI as the most powerful instrument we've ever built for understanding and designing the physical world. Materials are where that really becomes concrete.

If you look at the big problems we have, climate, energy, carbon capture, batteries, catalysts for green hydrogen, almost all of them bottleneck on materials. We need a material that absorbs CO2 efficiently and releases it cheaply, or a solid-state electrolyte that doesn't crack, or a catalyst that isn't made of platinum. And the way we discover materials today is still remarkably slow. It's a chemist with intuition, some trial and error in the lab, maybe a density functional theory calculation that takes days. The search space is astronomically large, and we've explored a tiny sliver of it.

What changed in the last few years is that the ingredients finally came together. We have equivariant neural networks that respect the physics, the symmetries of molecules and crystals, so they generalize instead of memorizing. We have generative models that can propose candidates rather than just screen them. We have foundation-model-style pretraining on simulation data. And crucially, we're learning how to close the loop: generate, simulate, test in the lab, feed the result back. That's the piece that makes it an engine rather than a one-off paper.

So for me CuspAI is about taking everything I've learned about building principled models and pointing it at something where success is measurable in a way that really matters. If we get it right, the output isn't a benchmark number, it's a material you can hold in your hand that pulls carbon out of the air. At this stage of my career, that's the kind of impact I want to work toward. I've written enough papers; now I'd like to help make the thing.

r001.rationale: The response cites climate and energy challenges and materials bottlenecks, but does not present political difficulty as a reason for pursuing technological solutions.

r002.rationale: Welling describes AI as a tool for understanding and designing the physical world and says he wants to apply it to materials with measurable, practical impact.

astra-6.text:
At this stage of my career, I’m interested in taking the ideas we develop in machine learning and using them to do something useful in the physical world. Materials science is a very compelling place to do that, because the properties of a material can make the difference between a technology that works in principle and one that is actually practical.

The exciting question is whether we can turn the discovery process around. Instead of starting with a material and asking what it does, can we start with the properties we need and ask what material would give us those properties? That brings together machine learning, physics, and chemistry in a very natural way.

For me, CuspAI is an opportunity to pursue that ambition with a concrete purpose. There are still difficult scientific problems to solve, but there is also the prospect of making something that matters. That combination is what attracts me.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention climate change or political difficulty as a reason for pursuing technological solutions.

r002.rationale: It says the attraction is combining difficult scientific problems with the prospect of making something that matters, and frames materials science as a way to apply machine learning in the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
What appeals to me is the opportunity to turn progress in AI into something tangible. Materials sit underneath so many important problems—energy, carbon capture, manufacturing—and finding better ones can have a real impact.

There’s also a fascinating scientific challenge. Rather than starting with a material and calculating its properties, you want to start with the properties you need and ask: what material would give me those? And can we actually make it? That brings together machine learning, simulation, and experiments.

For me, CuspAI is an opportunity to work on that whole loop. At this stage of my career, I’m excited by building something where the measure of success goes beyond a better benchmark score, to whether we can help solve a useful problem in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response mentions energy and carbon capture as important problems, but does not present political difficulty in addressing climate change as a reason for pursuing technological solutions.

r002.rationale: It describes materials discovery as a fascinating scientific challenge and emphasizes tangible impact on important real-world problems.
